cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-magnificat-virg.summary: In the upper left the Virgin Mary holds the Christ child up toward the Hand of God reaching from heaven: 'he hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy'. Around them the drawing pictures the Magnificat: an angel scatters the proud and pushes the mighty from their seats, the hungry approach a table to be filled with good things, and Abraham and his seed stand in the corner. It is an early image of Mary offering her Son.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-magnificat-virg.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

met:443592.summary: Woven in red and cream on this fragile band are the first events of Christ's life, set within little architectural frames and read from right to left: the Annunciation, the bathing of the newborn Christ, the Nativity with the Child lying in a stone manger, and the Adoration of the Shepherds. Though only fragments survive, the clear outlines of figures and buildings remain legible. A band like this may once have adorned a tunic, carrying the Gospel story on everyday dress.
facts: The Met notes that the bathing of the Christ Child was a popular motif not recorded in the Gospel texts.
It is woven in warp-faced compound twill of wool, linen and silk, and was made in Syria though found in Egypt.
The band came to the Met in 1890 as a gift of George F. Baker.

met:443592.notes: Scene identifications follow the Met; individual scenes are hard to make out in the small thumbnail.

vam:O115274.summary: This small hinged pendant cross once held a relic, probably a fragment of the True Cross, and was worn on the breast. Its front shows the crucified Christ in cloisonné enamel between busts of the Virgin and St John, with the sun and moon above and Adam's skull below; the side shown in the main photograph is the back, where the Virgin stands in prayer with raised hands, surrounded by busts of St John the Baptist, St Peter, St Andrew and St Paul on a translucent green ground.
facts: A contracted Greek inscription on the front gives Christ's words from the cross to his mother and the beloved disciple: 'Behold thy son! Behold thy mother!' (John 19:26–27). A large circular hole has since obliterated Christ's torso.
The cross is first recorded in the Debruge-Duménil collection in 1847; it then belonged to A. J. B. Beresford Hope, at whose sale at Christie's in May 1886 it was bought by the museum.

David Buckton used the translucent green background enamel to date it to the first phase of Byzantine cloisonné, between the end of Iconoclasm in 843 and about the mid-10th century; the V&A catalogues it as probably made in Italy, 800–900.
vam:O115274.notes: The worklist thumbnail (2008BU3893) shows the BACK of the cross (the Virgin orans with saints); Christ appears on the front. The V&A has a front view (image 2008BU3894: https://framemark.vam.ac.uk/collections/2008BU3894/full/!600,600/0/default.jpg), which would be a better image. Place of production debated (Italy vs Constantinople); the V&A says 'probably Italy'.

walters:71.113.summary: Under a pierced canopy carried on twisted columns, Christ hangs on the cross with arms spread wide and head inclined, while the Virgin raises her hands toward him and St John, holding a Gospel book, gestures in grief. At the foot of the cross a small rounded form, perhaps the skull of Adam, marks Golgotha. The figures have rounder faces and softer drapery than most ivories of their time.
facts: The Walters notes that the canopy and the softer, rounder style set this plaque apart from its contemporaries, and associates it with the Nikephoros Group, named after Emperor Nikephoros II.
Holes at each corner were used to fasten the wings of the triptych of which it was the centre.
walters:71.113.notes: The possible skull at the foot of the cross is my reading of the photograph; the museum does not mention it.
